<!-- Source: references/craft/cinematography.md -->
**Source: references/craft/cinematography.md**

# Craft — Cinematography

Lenses, camera bodies, movement, frame rate and depth: the choices that make an image read as photographed rather than generated. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## Why camera words work

Naming a real camera, lens and movement gives the model a concrete photographic target. "Shot on ARRI Alexa 35, 85mm prime" [Tested] carries more information than "cinematic, high quality".

```text
WEAK    Ultra realistic cinematic shot of a man in a bar.
STRONG  Shot on ARRI Alexa 35, 40mm anamorphic, handheld at shoulder height, shallow depth of field.
WHY     A real camera, lens and move replaces "realistic" with something to reproduce.
```

## Lenses (full-frame / Super 35 equivalents)

| Focal length | What it does | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| 14–18mm | exaggerated depth, distortion near the edges | claustrophobia, POV, cramped interiors, skate/action |
| 24mm | wide but natural; environment dominant | establishing, walking with a character |
| 32–35mm | human-eye width with context | persona selfie feel [Tested: 35mm prime], documentary, handheld drama |
| 40–50mm | neutral perspective | dialogue mediums, honest framing |
| 85mm | flattering compression, soft background | portraits and reference sheets [Tested: 85mm prime], close-ups |
| 100mm macro | texture at the micro scale | product details, skin texture, liquids |
| 135–200mm | heavy compression, stacked background | surveillance, heat-haze roads, isolation in crowds |

- **Anamorphic** [Tested as a Style DNA token]: oval bokeh, horizontal flares, a slight edge falloff. Reads as feature film. Pair it with 16:9.
- **Spherical primes** [Tested as a Style DNA token]: cleaner and more neutral. Good for product, documentary and polished commercial work.
- **Vintage glass** (softer contrast, glow on highlights): nostalgia, dreamlike memory.

## Camera bodies as look tokens

| Body | Read | Status |
|---|---|---|
| ARRI Alexa 35 | high-end cinema: natural skin, rich highlight roll-off | [Tested] for sheets, plates, cinematic Style DNA |
| Sony A7S III | polished creator / indie | [Tested] in the persona Style DNA |
| Recent smartphone | HDR, over-sharpening, noise, rolling shutter | [Tested] for raw UGC |
| Sony Venice 2, RED V-Raptor | high-end commercial and feature | General best practice |
| 16mm film (Arri SR3 / Bolex) | visible grain, gate weave, softer detail | General best practice |
| Super 8 | heavy grain, light leaks, home-movie memory | General best practice |
| VHS / MiniDV camcorder | interlaced softness, chroma noise, date stamps | General best practice. Good for found-footage horror |

Pick **one** body per project, and put it in the Style DNA so it repeats byte-identically.

## Camera movement

| Move | Feeling | Prompt mechanics |
|---|---|---|
| Locked-off / static | control, observation, deadpan | "locked-off on a tripod, no movement" |
| Handheld, subtle micro-shake [Tested] | immediacy, unease | "handheld with subtle micro-shake" |
| Handheld, human tremor (UGC) [Tested] | self-filmed authenticity | "natural hand tremor, small organic drifts, slightly crooked horizon" |
| Slow dolly push-in [Tested as a camera-style option] | realisation, intent, dread | "slow dolly push-in from MS to CU over the full 5 seconds" |
| Dolly pull-out | isolation, reveal of context | "dolly pulls back to reveal…" |
| Tracking / lateral | travel, momentum | "tracks alongside at walking pace, camera LEFT of subject" |
| Crane / jib up | scale, ending, release | "cranes up from ground level to an overhead wide" |
| Orbit / arc | spotlight, product hero | "slow 90-degree arc around the product, LEFT to RIGHT" |
| Whip pan | energy, a transition | "fast whip pan RIGHT, motion blur" |
| Rack focus | shifting attention | "focus racks from the glass in the foreground to @Image1 in the background" |
| Snap zoom | comedy, documentary urgency | "quick snap zoom into her eyes" |
| Gimbal / Steadicam float | dreamlike glide, luxury | Never use for UGC [Tested: no gimbal smoothness in UGC] |

Give every move a **speed**, a **start → end framing** and a **duration**. One move per shot is usually enough.

```text
WEAK    Dynamic camera movement around her.
STRONG  Slow 90-degree arc from her LEFT profile to full front, MS, over 5 seconds.
WHY     Direction, path, size and time are all specified; "dynamic" is not.
```

## Frame rate and shutter

- **24fps, 180-degree shutter** [Tested]: film motion cadence and natural motion blur. The cinematic default.
- **30fps** [Tested]: persona/creator content, and video-native feel.
- **Slow motion** (60–120fps conformed): write it explicitly only when intended. For UGC, write "never slow motion" [Tested], because models sometimes add it.

## Depth of field

- **Shallow**: isolates the subject, soft background. Portraits, emotion, product hero.
- **Deep focus** [Tested for plates]: everything sharp. Establishing shots, geography, location plates.
- State it per shot when it changes ("shallow depth of field on inserts, deep focus on wides" [Tested in the clean industrial Style DNA]).

## Framing principles

- Use thirds for natural framing, and centred symmetry for formality, menace or ritual.
- Headroom shrinks as shots tighten. In CUs, cutting the top of the head is fine; cutting the chin isn't.
- Leave lead room in the direction a subject looks or moves.
- Use foreground layers (a doorframe, a shoulder, a glass) to add depth and voyeurism.

## Cinematography checks

- [ ] One camera body and lens family for the whole project, in the Style DNA.
- [ ] Every shot names its lens or framing, plus a movement with direction and duration.
- [ ] Frame rate and shutter are in the Style DNA.
- [ ] Depth of field is stated where it matters.
- [ ] The movement style matches the playbook (smooth for product, human tremor for UGC).

# Craft — Lighting

Light is the main signal that separates photographed from generated. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## The rule [Tested]

Name the physical light source: what is producing the light, where it is, its colour and its quality. Never write "good lighting" or "cinematic lighting" without naming the source.

```text
WEAK    Dramatic lighting in the kitchen.
STRONG  A single warm under-cabinet strip as the key, soft falloff; cold blue pre-dawn light from a window just out of frame.
WHY     Two named sources with positions and colours give the model a real room to build.
```

## Describe every source with four properties

1. **Source**: a window, a tungsten lamp, an LED batten, a phone screen, a streetlight, firelight, the sun, an overcast sky.
2. **Position**: camera-LEFT or RIGHT, behind the subject, overhead, low; in frame (a practical) or just out of frame.
3. **Colour**: warm amber tungsten, neutral daylight, cold blue moonlight, sodium-vapour orange, magenta neon.
4. **Quality**: hard (sharp shadows, small source) or soft (large source, wrapped shadows); the falloff; the contrast.

## Setups and what they say

| Setup | Look | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| Motivated practical key | a lamp, screen or window in the scene is the main light | realism in any genre [Tested pattern] |
| Mixed colour temperature | warm practical against a cold window, the two sources visibly disagreeing | lived-in interiors, dawn and dusk realism [Tested] |
| Hard directional window daylight | long shadow bars across the floor | gyms, studios, drama, "propped phone in good light" [Tested] |
| Overcast ambient only | flat, soft, low contrast | bleak exteriors, documentary, northern realism [Tested] |
| Golden hour sun, low and behind | rim light, flare, warm haze | romance, nostalgia, lifestyle |
| Three-point (key, fill, back) | clean, controlled | interviews, corporate, product |
| Rembrandt (45° key, triangle on the far cheek) | sculpted, classical | drama portraits |
| Split light (90° side) | half the face in shadow | duality, threat, noir |
| Top light | eye sockets in shadow | interrogation, menace, sports halls |
| Backlight / silhouette | shape without detail | mystery, reveals, horror thresholds |
| Single-source darkness | one small source, everything else black | horror, suspense |
| Neon / coloured practicals | saturated pools, wet reflections | night city, music video |
| Firelight / candle | warm, flickering, very low | intimacy, period, ritual |
| Studio softbox at 45° + gentle fill | even, texture-revealing, no hard shadows | portraits and character sheets [Tested] |

## Lighting for reference images [Tested]

- **Portraits and character sheets**: soft even studio lighting from a large softbox key at 45 degrees with gentle fill, no hard shadows, no rim light, neutral white balance, against a plain mid-grey seamless backdrop.
- **Real-photo identity sheets**: soft, texture-revealing side-angle lighting on pure white seamless.
- **Location plates**: name the actual source, plus the colour disagreement if there is one. The plate's light becomes the video's light, so get it right here.

## Lighting in video blocks

- Keep the light consistent with the plate: "Match @Image3's window daylight and contrast exactly" [Tested pattern].
- Let the subject move through light: walking into a pool of window light exposes the face for the key line [Tested pattern].
- Motivate any change: a door opening, a lamp switched on, a cloud passing. Write the cause.

```text
WEAK    The lighting becomes more intense as tension builds.
STRONG  At 8 s the hallway bulb flickers twice and dies; only the phone screen lights her face from below.
WHY     A physical event changes the light; "intensity" is a mood.
```

## Lighting by material (product work)

- **Metal and car paint**: large soft sources make long clean highlights; dark flags shape the reflections.
- **Glass and liquids**: backlight or edge light so the liquid glows; a rim separates it from the background.
- **Matte surfaces**: a soft key at 45° and gentle fill, keeping the texture visible.
- **Skin**: soft key, small speculars, real pores visible. Never "flawless".

## Realism tells

- Real rooms are a little under-lit and uneven. "The room is under-lit and a little too dim" [Tested phrasing for phone realism].
- Highlights clip near windows in phone footage [Tested]. Cinema cameras roll off gently instead.
- Name what the light falls *on*: dust in the beam, steam, rain, chalk dust hanging in the light.

## Lighting checks

- [ ] Every light is a named physical source, with its position, colour and quality.
- [ ] Video light matches the plate, and any change has a cause.
- [ ] The setup fits the genre and the playbook (practical and imperfect for UGC; controlled for product).
- [ ] No "good", "cinematic" or "dramatic lighting" anywhere.

<!-- Source: references/craft/color-and-grade.md -->
**Source: references/craft/color-and-grade.md**

# Craft — Colour and Grade

Colour is decided twice: in generation, through the Style DNA and the plates, and in the edit, through the grade. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## Name it specifically [Tested]

Not "dark and moody". Name the values: where warm and cold sit (shadows, midtones, highlights), the saturation, the black level, the highlight behaviour, the grain and halation.

```text
WEAK    Dark, moody colour grade.
STRONG  Desaturated teal-green and grey, deep crushed blacks, cold blue-grey ambience.
WHY     Hue, saturation and black level are instructions; "moody" is an adjective.
```

## The palette sentence

Write the grade as one sentence covering four slots:

1. **Shadows**: crushed black · lifted milky black · cold blue shadows · warm amber shadows
2. **Midtones / skin**: natural skin · cool blue-grey midtones · warm golden midtones
3. **Highlights**: controlled highlights that never blow out · clipped highlights near windows (phone) · soft halation around practicals
4. **Saturation and texture**: desaturated · one saturated accent · fine 35mm grain · no grain

Example [Tested, persona Style DNA]: *warm amber shadows, cool blue-grey midtones, controlled highlights that never blow out, Kodak Vision3 250D character, subtle 35mm grain, soft halation around the practical light source.*

## Film stocks as colour tokens

| Token | Read | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Kodak Vision3 250D | daylight stock, balanced, gentle warmth | [Tested] in the persona Style DNA |
| Kodak Vision3 500T | tungsten stock, night, warm practicals, cooler ambient | General best practice |
| Kodak Vision3 50D | fine grain, saturated daylight | General best practice |
| Kodak Portra 400 (stills) | soft pastel skin, warm highlights | General best practice |
| Fuji Eterna (cine) | muted, slightly green-cyan, low contrast | General best practice |
| Kodak Ektachrome | punchy, saturated, slide-film contrast | General best practice |

## Recognisable looks and their mechanics

| Look | Mechanics |
|---|---|
| Bleak naturalism | desaturated teal-green and grey, crushed blacks, cold blue-grey ambience [Tested] |
| Phone-native realism | flat and ungraded, HDR, mild over-sharpening, luminance noise in shadows, clipped highlights [Tested] |
| Steel and graphite (product/car) | desaturated steel and graphite palette, deep blacks, cool blue-grey fill, hard key [Tested] |
| Near-monochrome with a warm pocket | charcoal and graphite with cool highlights on steel, one pocket of warm daylight [Tested, location plate pattern] |
| Warm nostalgia | lifted blacks, golden midtones, soft halation, 16mm grain |
| Night city | sodium-vapour orange against cyan shadows, saturated neon, wet reflections |
| Bleach bypass | low saturation, high contrast, silvery highlights. Grit, war, sci-fi |
| Clean commercial | neutral whites, accurate product colour, gentle contrast, no tint |

Avoid the generic teal-and-orange blockbuster grade unless it's asked for. It's the most "AI default" look, and naming it in a NEGATIVE line can help [Tested: "no cinematic or teal-and-orange grade" for phone looks].

## The one-accent rule [Tested pattern]

Keep the frame neutral or near-monochrome and let one element carry the only real colour, usually a wardrobe item or the product: *"the yellow raincoat is the only real colour in frame"*. It guides the eye and survives across blocks better than a global grade instruction.

## Grain, halation and texture

- Fine 35mm grain [Tested] is the cinematic default; 16mm grain is heavier and more nostalgic.
- Halation (a red-orange glow around bright practicals) reads as film [Tested in the persona Style DNA].
- Phone looks: **no** grain, no halation [Tested]. Put that in the NEGATIVE line, because models add film texture by default.

## Colour in plates vs blocks

- The location plate sets the colour reality. Write the palette into its `COLOUR GRADE:` line [Tested].
- Blocks repeat the palette through the Style DNA, byte-identical [Tested], and can add "Match @Image3's palette exactly" [Tested pattern].

## Grade in the edit [Tested]

- After Effects: apply the grade as a single adjustment layer across all clips.
- Add a subtle lens vignette.
- Add a 35mm grain overlay at 10–15% opacity if the generated grain feels insufficient.
- In CapCut for persona content, keep the grade minimal or flat.

## Colour checks

- [ ] The palette sentence names the shadows, midtones, highlights and texture.
- [ ] The plate's colour line and the Style DNA agree.
- [ ] Phone looks explicitly exclude grain, halation and cinematic grades.
- [ ] There's at most one saturated accent, if the look calls for one.

# Craft: sound, editing rhythm, continuity

Part of the AI Filmmaker knowledge set (files 00-09). When a section mentions a path such as
`references/craft/lighting.md`, search the knowledge files for "Source: references/craft/lighting.md".

---

<!-- Source: references/craft/sound-design.md -->
**Source: references/craft/sound-design.md**

# Craft — Sound Design

Sound sells reality more than image does. Generated native audio follows what you write, so write it like a sound designer. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## The rule [Tested]

Name specific sounds with their timing. Not "ambient sound", but *"rain on leaf litter, a low roll of thunder at 4 s, boots dragging through wet mud"*.

```text
WEAK    Audio: ambient office sounds.
STRONG  Audio: HVAC hum, a printer starting at 2 s, keys clattering two desks away, her chair creak at 5 s.
WHY     Named, located, timed sounds build a space; "ambient" builds nothing.
```

## Four layers of a soundtrack

1. **Room tone / ambience**: the space itself (fridge hum, distant traffic, fan, wind in pines). Always present; it glues the cuts.
2. **Hard effects / foley**: sounds of the action, synced (a scoop against plastic, a shaker lid, a bag zip, a barbell clang) [Tested examples of naming].
3. **Voice**: dialogue or voiceover, with a voice spec (see `directing-performance.md`).
4. **Music**: score or source music. Often added in the edit, not generated.

Write layers 1–3 in each shot's `Audio:` line. Decide layer 4 in the Bible and the edit plan.

## Native audio [Tested]

- Generate with native audio ON (Seedance 2.5) and keep it on top in the edit; lay music underneath.
- Every shot ends with an `Audio:` line.
- Microphone character is part of the realism. For phone content: *"slightly hot and a little clipped, like a phone mic in a reverberant room"* [Tested].

## Silence is a beat

- Write silence with a duration: *"no dialogue at all from 3 to 6 s — only breathing and equipment sound. That silence is deliberate; do not fill it."* [Tested pattern]
- Silence before a line or a reveal makes it land. A sudden absence of room tone is a horror tool.

## Music decisions

| Format | Default |
|---|---|
| UGC / persona | **No music** [Tested]. Room tone and silence carry authenticity; music signals "ad". |
| Cinematic | Score added in the edit, under native audio [Tested: music under the native audio track]. |
| Music video | The track goes on in the edit. Generated audio stays minimal or is replaced. |
| Product | Designed product sounds first (a click, a pour, an engine note), then music if the brand needs it. |

In generation, write "No music" explicitly when you don't want any [Tested], because models often add a score.

## Sound as storytelling

- **Off-screen sound** expands the world and creates dread: a door downstairs, a dog stopping barking.
- **Sound bridges / J-cuts**: the next shot's sound starts before the cut. Plan it in the edit, and write the sound early in the outgoing shot if needed.
- **Perspective**: distant vs close ("muffled through the wall", "right at the mic").
- **Sync points**: a clang, a slam or a click on a cut gives the edit snap.

## Voice in generation [Tested]

Always include a voice spec when someone speaks, identical across blocks:

> A natural, warm, human [female/male] voice, casual conversational cadence, real pitch variation, small natural imperfections. Must sound like an actual person, NOT synthetic or robotic.

For voiceover, write `Voiceover, no lip sync:` before the line.

## Output format — audio line

```
Audio: [room tone] · [synced effect at time] · [voice: "line" or none] · [music: none | as specified]
```

## Sound checks

- [ ] Every shot has an `Audio:` line with named sounds and timings.
- [ ] Music is decided (often "No music" in generation).
- [ ] Silence is written as a beat where it matters.
- [ ] A voice spec is present and identical, and voiceover is labelled.

---

<!-- Source: references/craft/editing-rhythm.md -->
**Source: references/craft/editing-rhythm.md**

# Craft — Editing and Rhythm

Rhythm is designed before generation, through shot durations and block splits, and finished in the edit. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## Durations are rhythm [Tested]

- Standard beat: 3–4 s. Travel, reveal or collapse: 5–6 s. Fast cut: 2 s. Under 2 s rarely renders cleanly.
- Shot durations must total the block length exactly.
- Blocks: 12–20 s target, 30 s hard ceiling, split at story beats.

```text
WEAK    0–3s, 3–6s, 6–9s, 9–12s, 12–15s  (all equal)
STRONG  0–5s establish · 5–7s reaction · 7–10s detail · 10–15s hold on the reveal
WHY     Varying lengths create acceleration and a landing; equal lengths drone.
```

## Rhythm patterns

| Pattern | Durations (15 s block) | Feeling |
|---|---|---|
| Slow build → hold | 5 / 3 / 3 / 4 | dread, revelation |
| Accelerate | 5 / 4 / 3 / 3 | rising energy, chase |
| Stutter + release | 3 / 2 / 2 / 8 | shock, then sit with it |
| Even observational | 4 / 4 / 3 / 4 | UGC, documentary |
| Beat-locked (120 BPM) | 4 / 2 / 2 / 4 / 3 | music video, bars of 2 s |

Music videos: at BPM *b*, one bar of 4/4 = 240 ÷ *b* seconds (120 BPM → 2 s, 90 BPM → 2.67 s). Cut on downbeats; save the longest hold for the drop.

## Cut on action [Tested]

Cut at the peak of a movement, not after it settles. In generation, overlap the action slightly across shots (the hand starts reaching at the end of shot A, completes the reach in shot B), so the edit has a cut point.

## Trims [Tested]

The first and last 10–15 frames of each generated block often have motion artifacts. Trim them in the edit. That means:
- Don't place key action in the first or last half-second of a block.
- Start each block with the action already settled, and end it with a described final frame (which feeds the next block's last-frame handoff).

## Endings and holds

- Let shots run slightly too long before cutting when you want discomfort or exhaustion [Tested pattern: "let this shot run slightly too long before cutting"].
- Hard cut mid-movement for abrupt UGC endings [Tested pattern: the clip cuts before the hand reaches the lens].
- For an image ending, hold 3–5 s with nothing new entering the frame.

## Dialogue editing [Tested]

- For persona content, sync dialogue cuts to natural breath breaks, not mid-sentence.
- Leave the silences in; don't tighten every pause.

## The edit pass, by tool [Tested]

**CapCut (persona / fast turnaround):** import blocks in order → trim heads and tails → cut on action → native audio on top, music under (usually none for UGC) → minimal or no grade → export.

**After Effects (cinematic):** assemble → a single adjustment-layer grade → subtle vignette → 35mm grain overlay at 10–15% if needed → minimal title cards (clean serif or sans-serif, never default fonts) → export.

**Export:** 1080p minimum, 4K if possible. YouTube: H.264, high bitrate. Instagram/TikTok: 9:16, H.265.

## Transitions

- Straight cuts by default. Every other transition must earn its place.
- Match cuts (shape, motion or colour) connect two blocks or locations elegantly. Plan the matching frames in the prompts.
- Use a sound bridge (J-cut, L-cut) to smooth a location change.
- Avoid generated "transition effects". Make transitions in the edit.

## Output format — edit plan

```
EDIT PLAN — [tool]
Order:   B1 → B2 → …
Trims:   B1 head __f / tail __f · …
Cuts:    [where, and on which action]
Holds:   [which shot runs long, and why]
Sound:   native audio on top · music [none | feel, level] · bridges
Grade:   [one adjustment layer: grade] · vignette · grain __%
Text:    [none | end card / titles, font, duration]
Export:  [aspect] · [resolution] · [codec]
```

## Rhythm checks

- [ ] Shot lengths vary deliberately, and the block lands on its longest or most important shot.
- [ ] No key action in the first or last ~0.5 s of a block.
- [ ] Block splits fall on story beats.
- [ ] The edit plan covers order, trims, cut points, sound, grade, text and export.

<!-- Source: references/craft/continuity.md -->
**Source: references/craft/continuity.md**

# Craft — Continuity

Across blocks, AI video forgets everything you don't restate. Continuity is a system of locks, hard facts and handoffs. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## The locks [Tested]

1. **Identity lock**: a character sheet per person and a reference per product, generated before any video.
2. **Space lock**: a location plate per setting, with no people.
3. **Look lock**: the Style DNA, pasted byte-identical into every block.
4. **Slot lock**: the @Image upload order, fixed for the whole project (characters → products → locations → last frame). The prompt binds to slots, not file names.
5. **Motion lock**: the final frame of block N, attached to block N+1.

```text
WEAK    Block 2: Mara continues walking down the same street as before.
STRONG  Block 2: @Image4 is the final frame of Block 1 — continue from it exactly. @Image1 walks on through @Image3.
WHY     "Same as before" means nothing to a model with no memory; the last frame does.
```

## Hard facts, restated in every block [Tested]

- **Sides**, in capitals: "the bandage is on his RIGHT hand", "the bag hangs from her LEFT shoulder". Models mirror references constantly.
- **Wardrobe state**: what is on, what is off, and what must NOT appear ("the jacket is already off and must not appear").
- **Condition**: wet, muddy, wounded, sweating, and exactly where.
- **Props**: who holds what, in which hand.
- **Time and weather**: these persist unless the script changes them.
- **Face source**: "In each character sheet, take the face from the chest-up portrait panel. The centre panel omits the head deliberately." [Tested]

## Progression across blocks [Tested pattern]

When something changes over time (sweat building, rain soaking clothes, light fading), write the start state, the end state and the direction:

```text
STRONG  Over this block @Image1 goes from dry to soaked: rain darkens the coat shoulders first, then the hair flattens against the forehead.
WHY     Start, end and location of the change; the model interpolates instead of inventing.
```

Then the next block starts from that end state.

## The last-frame handoff [Tested]

1. End each block on a described, stable frame: "END ON THIS FRAME — [pose, position in frame, wardrobe state, light]".
2. After generating, save that frame as a still.
3. Attach it as the last slot of the next block, and open that block with: "This clip picks up seconds after the previous one."

## Screen direction and geography

- Keep characters on consistent sides of the frame within a scene, and state it in every block.
- Exits and entrances match: out frame RIGHT, in from frame LEFT.
- Direction of travel is a hard fact for vehicles and walks.

## Continuity ledger (keep it in the Bible)

```
CONTINUITY
@Image1: bandage RIGHT hand · grey hoodie ON (Block 1) → OFF (Block 2+) · hair wet from Block 2
@Image2 (product): label always faces camera, cap ON until 0:22
Time: dusk → full dark by Block 3 · rain: continuous
Screen: @Image1 frame LEFT, @Image3 frame RIGHT in the kitchen scene
```

## Common breaks and fixes

| Break | Fix |
|---|---|
| Face changes between blocks | Never change the upload order; attach the last frame from block 2 onward [Tested] |
| Location looks different | The same plate in every block, plus "match @ImageN" [Tested] |
| Prop jumps hands | State the hand in every block, in capitals |
| Wardrobe reappears | Say what must not appear, and add it to NEGATIVE |
| Light or colour shifts | Byte-identical Style DNA [Tested]; one grade layer in the edit [Tested] |

## Continuity checks

- [ ] Every block declares the full @Image set in Bible order, and blocks 2+ include the last frame.
- [ ] The sides, wardrobe, condition and props in each block match the ledger.
- [ ] Every block except the last ends on a described frame.
- [ ] Each progression has a start state, an end state and a location.

Part of the AI Filmmaker knowledge set (files 00-09). When a section mentions a path such as
`references/craft/lighting.md`, search the knowledge files for "Source: references/craft/lighting.md".

---

<!-- Source: references/translation/image-prompts.md -->
**Source: references/translation/image-prompts.md**

# Translation — Image Prompts (Reference Images)

Output formats for the Stage 3 reference images: portraits, character sheets, product references and location plates. **You** fill these in for the user's project and deliver each one in its own code block. Never show them blank.

These images exist to **lock** identity and space before any video [Tested]. Every later video prompt says "match @ImageN" instead of re-describing.

## Filling rules (apply to every format)

- **Specific and ordinary beats beautiful.** The more ordinary and precise a face description is, the more real it looks [Tested].
- **Sides are the character's own LEFT/RIGHT**, in capitals. Add the line "Body sides marked LEFT or RIGHT are the character's own left and right, not the viewer's" whenever a side is mentioned.
- **Light names its source** [Tested]. For plates, the light you write becomes the video's light.
- **Always include a realism clause and a camera** [Tested]: a real body and lens, "visible skin texture and pores, no retouching", "NOT a digital render, NOT a 3D visualisation".
- **Original characters**: add "Original character, not resembling any existing person or public figure" unless the user supplied real photos of a person who has consented.
- Remove every `[bracket]`, and delete optional lines that don't apply.

```text
WEAK    A beautiful young woman with perfect skin and nice hair.
STRONG  Light olive skin with a warm undertone, slightly uneven; oval face; dark brown almond eyes; thick, slightly unruly brows; faint flush across the nose.
WHY     Ordinary specifics produce a person; "beautiful" produces the model's average face.
```

---

## 1. Portrait — 4:5 [Tested]

Generate this first and get the face exactly right before making the sheet. Label line: `Nano Banana Pro · 4:5 · portrait for [Name] (attach to the sheet prompt next)`

```
Photorealistic character reference photograph. Chest-up portrait of a [AGE]-year-old [woman/man/person] against a plain mid-grey seamless studio backdrop, facing camera straight on.

FACE: [Skin tone and undertone. Face shape and jaw. Eye colour and shape. Nose. Lips. Brows. Any distinctive features, with the side in capitals.]

HAIR: [Colour. Length. Texture. Style. Condition: dry / wet / tied up / messy.]

BUILD: [Visible from the chest up: neck, shoulders, posture.]

WARDROBE: [Top layer visible from the chest up: garment, fabric, colour, condition.]

EXPRESSION: [What a camera sees, e.g. "relaxed, mouth closed, lips resting together, eyes calm and steady into the lens".]

CONDITION: [Clean / wet / wounded / dirty, and exactly where.]

DISTINGUISHING FEATURE: [Tattoo, scar, glasses, earrings, with location; or "None — no tattoos, jewellery or glasses."]

Background: plain mid-grey seamless studio backdrop, completely empty, evenly lit, no texture, no gradient, no shadow cast on the backdrop.

Shot on ARRI Alexa 35, 85mm prime lens, soft even studio lighting from a large softbox key at 45 degrees with gentle fill, no hard shadows, no rim light, neutral white balance, sharp focus throughout, visible skin texture and pores, no retouching, fine film grain. Original character, not resembling any existing person or public figure.

NEGATIVE: no smooth or airbrushed skin, no beauty filter, no CGI look, no gradient background, no heavy makeup, no resemblance to any real person.
```

## 2. Three-panel character sheet — 16:9, headless centre [Tested, primary method]

Attach the approved portrait as a reference. This image becomes the character's @Image slot. Label line: `Nano Banana Pro · 16:9 · attach approved portrait · becomes @Image[N]`

**Why the headless centre panel:** it leaves exactly one face on the sheet. If two full faces appear, the video model averages them into a blurred, unstable identity. One face, used twice, locks the model onto a single identity that holds across blocks [Tested].

```
Photorealistic character reference sheet. Three panels side by side against a plain mid-grey seamless studio backdrop. One continuous background across all three panels. Match the attached approved portrait exactly — same face, same skin, same hair.

LEFT PANEL — chest-up portrait of a [AGE]-year-old [woman/man/person], facing camera straight on, level chin, calm neutral expression, eyes into the lens.
FACE: [paste the portrait's FACE description]
HAIR: [paste the portrait's HAIR description]
WARDROBE (TOP LAYER ONLY): [top garment]

CENTRE PANEL — full-length front view of the same [woman/man/person], framed from the shoulders down so the head is DELIBERATELY CROPPED OUT OF FRAME. This is an intentional headless costume display — the clothing simply stops at the collar line. The omission is deliberate so the model locks onto one single face from the LEFT panel only.
Standing upright and square to camera, weight evenly on both feet, arms hanging relaxed and straight at the sides, nothing crossing the body, hands open and visible.
BUILD: [height and build, head to toe]
WARDROBE, HEAD TO TOE: [top, bottom, footwear, condition]
DISTINGUISHING FEATURES: [tattoos, jewellery, with the side in capitals]

RIGHT PANEL — full-length rear three-quarter view of the same [woman/man/person], seen mostly from behind, HEAD FULLY VISIBLE AND COMPLETE from the top of the skull down to the feet. Hair, skull shape and nape of the neck all in frame. Head turned very slightly so a sliver of cheek or jaw catches in profile.
HAIR FROM BEHIND: [how the hair sits from behind]
WARDROBE FROM BEHIND: [the same outfit from behind, identical colour, fabric and condition]
Same neutral upright posture, arms at sides.

CRITICAL: Only the CENTRE panel is headless. LEFT and RIGHT panels both include the head. This character has a head and face in every shot of the film.

All three panels identically lit and identically scaled. Plain mid-grey seamless studio backdrop, completely empty, evenly lit, no texture, no gradient.

Shot on ARRI Alexa 35, 85mm prime lens, soft even studio lighting from a large softbox key at 45 degrees with gentle fill, no hard shadows, no rim light, neutral white balance, sharp focus throughout, visible skin texture and pores, no retouching, fine film grain. Original character, not resembling any existing person or public figure.

NEGATIVE: no resemblance to any real person or influencer, no identity drift between panels, no smooth or airbrushed or waxy or CGI-looking skin, no beauty filter, no heavy makeup, no arched back or posed stance, no action poses, no hands raised, no crossed arms, no props, no text, no watermark, no branding.
```

Optional name label [Tested]: replace "no text" with *A small, clean white sans-serif label in the top-left corner of the LEFT panel reads "[NAME]", with "AGE [N]" in smaller type beneath it. No other text anywhere on the sheet.*

**Alternative — turnaround plus separate full-length shots [Tested]:** a chest-up turnaround (front / profile / back, one image), with the headless full-length front and the full-length rear three-quarter view generated as **separate** 16:9 images. Use it when the model won't render the headless centre panel correctly in one image. The trade-off: the profile panel adds a second face angle. Keep the front panel as the clear face source, and say so in every block.

## 3. Real person — four-photo identity lock [Tested]

Use this when the user uploads four photos of the same real person (with their consent). The four photos occupy the reference slots during sheet generation only.

```
CRITICAL IDENTITY LOCK: @Image1, @Image2, @Image3, and @Image4 are all photos of the exact same real person. This is not a composite or blended face. They must be immediately and unmistakably recognizable as the specific individual shown — with their exact face shape, exact eye shape and colour, exact nose, exact lips, exact eyebrow shape, exact jawline, exact skin tone, and exact hair colour, texture, and length as shown. Do not average, generalize, beautify, or drift toward a generic model-like face. If any single reference is clearer than the others, prioritize matching that one exactly rather than blending all four into something new.

A four-panel character reference sheet: front / three-quarter / side / face and texture detail.

Wardrobe: [outfit]

Pure white seamless background across all four panels. Soft texture-revealing side-angle lighting. Real skin texture, never airbrushed.

NEGATIVE: no identity drift from the uploaded references under any circumstances, no generic or composite or averaged face, no beautification, no smooth or airbrushed or CGI-looking skin.
```

Note: this route shows four face angles, which is the opposite of the headless-panel logic. It's documented as tested for real people. If identity averages in video, fall back to generating a headless three-panel sheet from the best front photo.

## 4. Skin realism pass [Tested]

Run this as an edit on the approved sheet, only if the skin looks too perfect. Label line: `Nano Banana Pro · edit on the approved sheet · same aspect ratio`

```
Take this exact image and increase skin and overall realism only. Keep the same identity, pose, outfit, panel layout, background, and lighting exactly as shown.

SKIN REALISM: replace any smooth, airbrushed, or beauty-filter skin with genuinely photographed skin texture — real visible pores across the forehead, cheeks and nose, subtle natural uneven tone, faint texture irregularities. The character should still look [attractive / natural / weathered] but through real photographic texture, not a smoothed surface.

NEGATIVE: no smooth, plastic, waxy, glass-smooth, or CGI-rendered skin. No beauty filter. No change to face shape, identity, pose, wardrobe, or background.
```

## 5. Product reference — 16:9 [General best practice]

The tested part is the principle: a product gets its own reference image so close-ups match it instead of reinventing it. The prompt pattern below is derived, not tested. Label line: `Nano Banana Pro · 16:9 · becomes @Image[N] (product)`

```
Photorealistic product reference photograph, 16:9. [PRODUCT] [and ACCESSORY] standing side by side on a pure white seamless background, centred, straight-on front view at product height, label facing camera.

PRODUCT: [exact shape and proportions, size cue, material and finish (matte / gloss / brushed metal / clear plastic), precise colour names, cap or lid, transparent parts and what is visible through them]

LABEL: [exact wording — keep it short], [clean sans-serif wordmark / other style], [colour], [position on the pack]. Lettering crisp, correctly spelled, perfectly flat to the surface.

ACCESSORY: [optional: shaker, case, box, with the same level of detail]

Lighting: large soft overhead and frontal softboxes, even and shadowless except a soft contact shadow beneath each object, true-to-life colour, controlled reflections that never cross the label.

Shot on a medium-format stills camera, 100mm macro lens at f/8, deep focus, everything sharp. This must read as an actual product photograph — NOT a 3D render, NOT a CGI packshot.

NEGATIVE: no extra text, no misspelled or warped lettering, no other logos, no real-world brand marks, no props, no hands, no gradient background, no reflections over the label.
```

Optional extra views [General best practice]: generate the three-quarter view, the back, and a label/texture macro as **separate** images, keeping the front view as the product's main @Image slot. Separate images avoid several tiny labels on one sheet, which is where text warps.

```text
WEAK    A sleek premium protein tub with a cool logo.
STRONG  Matte black cylindrical tub, ribbed black screw lid, single white wordmark "KORE" centred low on the front, nothing else printed.
WHY     Shape, finish, colour and exact text give the model one product to hold.
```

## 6. Location plate — no people [Tested]

One plate per setting. Lock the location before the video so the video model only has to handle performance, not invent a location and its lighting at the same time. Default aspect ratio: 16:9 [Tested, including for 9:16 projects]. Matching the project's aspect ratio is a [General best practice] alternative when exact vertical framing matters. Label line: `Nano Banana Pro · 16:9 · becomes @Image[N] (location)`

```
[Photorealistic cinematic establishing plate / Photorealistic interior photograph / Real phone photo], [wide shot / three-quarter angle]. No people. Empty of people entirely.

SETTING: [type of space, with specific materials and wear]
ERA / STYLE: [contemporary / 1970s / brutalist / cluttered and lived-in]
TIME OF DAY: [pre-dawn / golden hour / overcast noon / late dusk / night]
WEATHER (exterior only): [heavy rain / fog / dry / clear]

KEY ELEMENTS: [every object that must appear, with its frame position — foreground / mid-ground / background, LEFT / centre / RIGHT of frame]

LIGHTING: [the actual physical light source(s): position, colour temperature, quality, and whether the sources disagree in colour]

COLOUR GRADE: [the palette sentence: shadows, midtones, highlights, texture]

CAMERA POSITION: [height and angle, and what it looks at — e.g. "low at hip height, three-quarter angle looking down the length of the floor"]

MOOD: [one line — a coherence check for you; it doesn't instruct the model]

This must read as an actual photograph taken [on a phone in a real space / on a real camera] — NOT a digital render, NOT a 3D visualisation, NOT a video-game environment, NOT an AI-generated look.

Shot on [ARRI Alexa 35 / Sony A7S III / a recent smartphone], [focal length], [deep focus / shallow], [35mm grain / no grain for phone looks], [natural light only / mixed practical sources].

NEGATIVE: no people, no text, no logos, no CGI or 3D render look, no flat or shadowless lighting, [no plants / no clutter unless specified], [anything specific to avoid].
```

```text
WEAK    A gritty laundromat at night with nice lighting.
STRONG  Row of steel washers mid-ground LEFT; orange plastic chairs foreground RIGHT; one flickering fluorescent tube overhead as the only key; wet night street through the window behind.
WHY     Objects with frame positions and a named light become a set the video can return to.
```

**Phone-look plates** [Tested]: say "real phone photo", ask for an under-lit room, mild noise in the shadows and mismatched practical light, and put "no film grain, no halation, no cinematic colour grade, no even or flattering lighting" in the NEGATIVE.

**Two plates for one space** [Tested pattern]: a wide establishing plate for arrivals, and a tighter plate of the exact corner where the action happens.

## Image-prompt checks

- [ ] Aspect ratio and label line above every code block.
- [ ] The sheet has exactly one full face and states that only the centre panel is headless.
- [ ] Every side is in capitals, with the "character's own left and right" line.
- [ ] Plates contain no people, and every key element has a frame position.
- [ ] A realism clause, a camera body and lens, and a NEGATIVE line in every prompt.
- [ ] No brackets left unfilled.

---

<!-- Source: references/translation/video-prompts.md -->
**Source: references/translation/video-prompts.md**

# Translation — Video Prompts (Block Prompts)

How to turn the script, the shot list and the director's judgment into generation-ready block prompts. The rules and formats here are **[Tested]** with Seedance 2.5 (omni_reference mode on OpenArt) unless marked. For other video models, keep the craft and check the model's own limits; never assume they match.

## Hard rules [Tested]

- Every block is 30 seconds or less. Target 12–20 seconds per block.
- Split blocks at story beats, never mid-moment.
- Timestamps restart at 0 inside each block.
- Shot durations: 3–4 s for most beats, 5–6 s for travel or reveals, 2 s for a fast cut. Under 2 s rarely renders.
- Shot durations must total the block length exactly.

**Montage exception** [Tested]: several fast cuts can live inside one timestamped segment of at least 2 s, if labelled: `0–3s: MONTAGE, three quick cuts: (a) … (b) … (c) …`.

**Timestamp format**: write `0–4s:`, `4–7s:`, `7–9.5s:`. Half seconds are fine. Use the same format in every block.

## Craft rules [Tested] — apply without being asked

- **Camera first** in every shot: position and movement, then subject, then action, then atmosphere. Early tokens carry more weight.
- **Physical actions only**, never interior states.
- **Sustained poses need a duration**: "holds the aim for the full three seconds and does not lower the arm".
- **Involuntary motion needs a mechanism**: "his hand goes limp, fingers uncurl, it slips from a slack grip".
- **Name the wrong version inline** when a mistake is likely: "— he does not open his hand, does not throw it".
- **LEFT/RIGHT are hard facts**, capitalised, in every block.
- **Style DNA is written once** and pasted byte-identical as the last section of every block.
- **Write cinematically, never clinically**: full sentences with texture, not keyword lists.
- **Refer to people and products by @Image number.** A name may appear only attached to its tag ("Mara @Image1"), never on its own.

```text
WEAK    Mara walks in, nervous, close-up, rain, cinematic.
STRONG  Handheld close-up, 50mm, tracking backward. Mara @Image1 walks in out of the rain, water running off her hood; her eyes check the room LEFT to RIGHT.
WHY     Camera → subject → action → atmosphere, in sentences, with a tag and a visible behaviour.
```

## @Image binding

- Declare every slot the block uses at the top, in Bible order, each with a one-line description and a "match" instruction.
- Keep the slot numbers fixed for the whole project. Upload the same images in the same order for every block, even if a block doesn't mention every slot [General best practice: keeps numbering stable].
- Character sheets always get the face-source line [Tested]: *"In each character sheet, take the face from the chest-up portrait panel (LEFT). The centre panel omits the head deliberately. [Characters] have a head and face in every shot."*
- Products: *"@Image2 — the [product]. Match exactly: [shape, colour, finish, label]."* [Tested]
- Locations: *"@Image3 — [space]. Match the [light source], palette and contrast exactly."* [Tested]
- Blocks 2+: *"@Image[N] — final frame of Block [N-1]. Continue from it exactly."* [Tested]

```text
WEAK    Use the reference images for the characters and the place.
STRONG  @Image1 — character sheet, ODE. Take the face from the LEFT portrait panel; the centre panel omits the head deliberately. Match exactly.
WHY     Slot, role, face source and instruction in one line; nothing left to interpret.
```

## Dialogue, voiceover and audio

- On camera: the speaker is still when speaking. `@Image1 stops at the counter. Beat. She says, flat: "Not tonight."` [Tested rule]
- Voiceover over action: `Voiceover, no lip sync: "…"` [Tested]
- Silence: write it with a duration and say not to fill it [Tested pattern].
- Audio: either one `Audio:` line per shot (standard format) or a global `AUDIO:` section plus synced sounds written into the shot text (UGC format). Both are tested. Never write "ambient sound".
- Voice spec whenever anyone speaks, identical in every block (see `craft/directing-performance.md`).

## Realism clause [Tested]

If the look drifts toward CGI, add to the block: *"This must read as actual footage shot on a real camera, NOT a digital render, NOT a 3D visualization, NOT a video game environment."*

---

## Output format A — standard block (cinematic, product, drama) [Tested]

Label line: `Seedance 2.5 · omni_reference · [9:16 | 16:9] · Block [N] of [T] · upload @Image1–[K] in order`

```
BLOCK [N] — [start]–[end] — [BEAT NAME]

@Image1 = [character 1 — one line: name, key physical detail, wardrobe]
@Image2 = [character 2 / product — one line]
@Image3 = [location — one line: space, time of day, key light]
@Image4 = [final frame of Block N-1 — blocks 2+ only]

In each character sheet, take the face from the LEFT chest-up portrait panel. The centre panel omits the head deliberately. [Name(s)] [has/have] a head and face in every shot of this film.

Continuous scene. [No dialogue / Voiceover only / Dialogue on camera]. [Weather]. [Time of day].
[LEFT/RIGHT facts: "The wound is on the LEFT arm. The torch is in the RIGHT hand."]
[Blocks 2+: "This clip picks up seconds after the previous one. Continue from @Image4 exactly."]

0–[X]s: [Camera position, lens, movement]. [@ImageN subject] [exact physical action]. [Atmosphere detail].
Audio: [specific sounds with timing]

[X]–[Y]s: Cut. [Camera]. [@ImageN subject]. [Action]. [Atmosphere].
Audio: [specific sounds]

[... until the durations total the block length]

[Not the final block: "END ON THIS FRAME — [pose, frame position, wardrobe state, light]."]

NEGATIVE: [likely failures for this block: identity drift, CGI look, slow motion, text, extra people, the wrong version of key actions]

Style DNA:
[paste byte-identical from the Bible]
```

## Output format B — UGC / persona block [Tested pattern]

The same rules, with performance and capture direction up front. Label line as above.

```
BLOCK [N] — [start]–[end] — [BEAT NAME]

@Image1 — character sheet, [NAME]. Take the face from the LEFT chest-up portrait panel. The centre panel omits the head deliberately. [Name] has a head and face in every shot. [Name] matches the sheet 100% — exact face, exact skin texture, exact hair, exact build, exact wardrobe. One specific real person, not a composite. Do not beautify, smooth, or drift toward a generic face.
@Image2 — the [product]. Match exactly: [shape, colour, label].
@Image3 — [location]. Match the [light] exactly.
[@Image4 — final frame of Block N-1 — blocks 2+ only]

[Blocks 2+: CONTINUITY — CRITICAL. This clip picks up seconds after the previous one. Wardrobe now: [state]; [item] is already off and must not appear. Over this clip [Name] progresses from [start state] to [end state].]

CAMERA: every frame filmed on a phone, held at arm's length by [Name] or propped on a surface. Genuine handheld feel — real hand tremor, small organic drifts, slightly crooked horizons. Never a tripod, never a gimbal, never slow motion.
PACING: dialogue and physical action never overlap. [Name] speaks, or moves — never both. Leave real silence between lines.
PERFORMANCE: [energy as behaviour — e.g. low energy, underselling, talking to the phone like to a friend, no smiling at the lens].

0–[X]s · [BEAT]. [Camera setup]. [Name] @Image1 [action]. [She/He] says, [delivery]: "[line]". [Pause or beat.]
[X]–[Y]s · [BEAT]. Cut. [Camera]. [Hands-only insert / action]. Voiceover, no lip sync: "[line]". [Sounds of the action.]
[...]

VOICE: [voice spec — identical in every block].
AUDIO: [room tone, action sounds, mic character]. No music.
NEGATIVE: [identity drift, airbrushed skin, tripod or gimbal smoothness, slow motion, film grain or cinematic grade if phone look, music, on-screen text, robotic voice, dialogue overlapping action, enthusiasm, other people, real brand logos, watermark].

Style DNA:
[paste byte-identical from the Bible]
```

---

## From script to blocks: procedure

1. Mark the beats in the script, and group them into blocks of 12–20 s at beat boundaries.
2. For each block, write the director's judgment (beat, shots, lens/light logic, rhythm, sound).
3. Assign durations so they total the block exactly. Vary them for rhythm (`craft/editing-rhythm.md`).
4. Write each shot camera-first, using the visible behaviour from the script's [brackets].
5. Move dialogue so it never overlaps movement. Convert lines over action to labelled voiceover, or split the shot.
6. Add LEFT/RIGHT facts, continuity lines and the END ON THIS FRAME line.
7. Add NEGATIVE, then paste the Style DNA last.
8. Run the quality gate, and `scripts/validate_blocks.py` if you can run code.

## Video-prompt checks

- [ ] Header with number, time range and beat.
- [ ] All slots declared in Bible order, with the face-source line and match instructions.
- [ ] Durations: starting at 0, contiguous, totalling the block length, ≥2 s per segment, block ≤30 s.
- [ ] Camera first in every shot, physical actions only, and holds with durations.
- [ ] No on-camera dialogue during movement, and voiceover labelled.
- [ ] Audio named and timed, and a voice spec where anyone speaks.
- [ ] END ON THIS FRAME in every block but the last.
- [ ] Style DNA last and byte-identical.

<!-- Source: references/models/seedance-2.5.md -->
**Source: references/models/seedance-2.5.md**

# Model — Seedance 2.5 (video)

ByteDance's video model, used in this workflow on **OpenArt** in **omni_reference** mode. Everything marked **[Tested]** comes from real productions with this setup. Everything marked **[General best practice]** comes from public reports or general experience and has not been tested here. Pass these labels on to the user.

## Settings — use these every time [Tested]

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Platform | OpenArt |
| Model | Seedance 2.5 |
| Mode | omni_reference |
| Aspect ratio | 9:16 (vertical) or 16:9 (cinematic) |
| Resolution | 1080p |
| Duration | the block length, 30 seconds max per block |
| Bitrate | Standard |
| Native audio | ON |

Setting names and options can differ on other platforms that host Seedance. Ask the user what their interface shows rather than assuming.

## Limits and timing [Tested]

- 30 s maximum per block; target 12–20 s.
- Shots under 2 s rarely render cleanly. Standard beats are 3–4 s, travel and reveals 5–6 s, fast cuts 2 s.
- Timestamps restart at 0 inside each block, and shot durations must total the block length exactly.
- Early tokens carry more weight, so camera position and movement come first in every shot.
- The first and last 10–15 frames of a block often have motion artifacts, which get trimmed in the edit.

## Reference images [Tested]

- Prompts refer to uploaded images as `@Image1`, `@Image2`, … in upload order. **The prompt binds to slots, not to file names.**
- Never change the upload order across generations. If the order changes, the wrong reference gets the wrong role.
- Order rule: characters → products → locations → the final frame of the previous block (blocks 2+). Numbered without gaps and fixed for the project.
- Character sheets with a headless centre panel give the model exactly one face to lock onto. Two full faces get averaged into a blurred identity.
- Attaching the previous block's final frame from Block 2 onward is the main defence against face and location drift.

Public reports say Seedance 2.5 accepts up to about 30 reference images in one generation, plus video and audio references [General best practice: public spec, not tested here]. In this workflow, projects used up to 6 image slots.

## Generation order [Tested]

1. Generate Block 1. Review identity consistency, lighting match and motion quality.
2. Save the final frame of Block 1 as a still.
3. Generate Block 2 with that still attached in the last-frame slot.
4. Repeat for every block.

## What the model responds to [Tested]

- Camera bodies, lenses, frame rates and named grades in a byte-identical Style DNA.
- Explicit realism clauses ("actual footage shot on a real camera, NOT a digital render, NOT a 3D visualization").
- Physical action described as mechanics, with durations for held poses.
- Explicit negatives for common drift: slow motion, gimbal smoothness, beauty filters, film grain on phone looks, music.
- Specific, timed sounds in `Audio:` lines. Native audio follows them.
- A voice spec ("natural, warm, human… NOT synthetic or robotic") to avoid robotic voices.

## Known failure modes and fixes [Tested]

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| Face changes between blocks | Check the upload order; attach the last frame from block 2 onward |
| Looks like a 3D render | Add the realism clause |
| Character does two things at once | Separate the actions into separate shots; dialogue and action never overlap |
| "Drops it" renders as a throw | Describe the mechanism and name the wrong version |
| Plastic skin | Run the skin realism pass on the sheet before generating video |
| Block too long or too short | Count the shot durations; they must total the block exactly |
| Location differs between blocks | Attach the same plate in every block and reference it |
| Robotic voice | Add the voice spec |
| Glitchy very short shot | Merge it with the adjacent shot or extend it to 3 s |

For anything else, see `troubleshooting.md`.

## Public information, not tested here [General best practice]

- Public reports put Seedance 2.5's release around mid-2026, with single generations of up to about 30 s and a maximum output of 1080p. Claims of native 4K output did not ship, according to reviews.
- Availability varies by region and platform.
- Some platforms expose editing and extension features. This workflow hasn't tested them, so suggest a short test before relying on them.

## Never claim

- That Seedance will lip-sync to an uploaded song, accept a specific number of references on the user's platform, render readable small text, or keep identity without reference images. None of these is tested here.
- Any setting the user's interface doesn't show.

---

<!-- Source: references/models/nano-banana-pro.md -->
**Source: references/models/nano-banana-pro.md**

# Model — Nano Banana Pro (images)

Google's image model (Gemini 3 Pro Image), used in this workflow for every reference image: portraits, character sheets, product references and location plates. **[Tested]** marks what real productions proved; **[General best practice]** marks public information or general experience.

## Order of operations — never skip a step [Tested]

1. **Portrait** (4:5). Review and fix the face. Don't move on until the face is right.
2. **Three-panel character sheet** (16:9), generated with the approved portrait attached as a reference. Review identity consistency across the panels.
3. **Skin realism pass** (an edit on the approved sheet), only if the skin looks smooth, waxy or airbrushed.
4. **Product reference(s)** (16:9) and **location plates** (16:9). Review the lighting and key elements.
5. **Save** every approved image with a clear name: `portrait-[name].png`, `sheet-[name].png`, `product-[name].png`, `plate-[place].png`.

## Aspect ratios [Tested]

| Image | Ratio |
|---|---|
| Portrait | 4:5 |
| Character sheet | 16:9 |
| Location plate | 16:9 (also used for vertical 9:16 projects) |
| Product reference | 16:9 |

## What works [Tested]

- Real camera language in image prompts: "Shot on ARRI Alexa 35, 85mm prime lens, soft even studio lighting from a large softbox key at 45 degrees with gentle fill".
- A plain mid-grey seamless backdrop for invented characters, and pure white seamless for real-photo identity sheets.
- "Visible skin texture and pores, no retouching, fine film grain" plus a NEGATIVE line against airbrushed, beauty-filter or CGI skin.
- Attaching the approved portrait when generating the sheet, so the face carries over.
- Follow-up edits on an approved image ("Take this exact image and … keep the same identity, pose, outfit, panel layout, background, and lighting exactly as shown").
- A short name label on the sheet, when requested, as one clean sans-serif line plus a smaller age line.
- Location plates with every key object placed by frame position, and named, physically motivated light.

## Watch for [Tested]

- **Too-perfect skin**: run the skin realism pass.
- **A second face sneaking into the sheet**, or the headless centre panel getting a head: regenerate, or switch to the alternative (generate the full-length panels as separate images).
- **Identity drift between panels**: re-attach the portrait and repeat "match the attached approved portrait exactly".

## Public information, not tested here [General best practice]

- Public reports say Nano Banana Pro accepts up to 14 reference images and outputs at 1K, 2K or 4K. Lists of supported aspect ratios vary by platform.
- **Nano Banana 2** (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, released February 2026) is a newer, faster sibling. This workflow hasn't tested it. If the user prefers it, use the same prompts and review the results with the same checklist.
- Text rendering is generally strong for image models of this class, but keep label text short and check the spelling on every product reference.

## Never claim

- A specific reference-image limit or resolution on the user's platform. Ask, or label it as a public report.
- That an image prompt guarantees identity. Always tell the user what to check before approving.

# Style DNA Library

The Style DNA is the visual signature of a project: written once, locked in the Production Bible, and pasted **byte-identical** as the last section of every video block [Tested]. Never reword it between blocks, not even a synonym.

## The structure [Tested]

```
Style DNA:
Shot on [camera body] with [anamorphic / spherical] prime lenses. [Camera movement style]. Photoreal live-action cinematography, no stylisation. [Key light source, named]. [Colour palette in specifics: shadows, midtones, highlights]. [Persistent atmosphere: weather, haze, lens effects]. [Frame rate]fps, 180-degree shutter, [grain], [depth of field]. [Tone words from the brief].
```

Rules:
- Mechanisms only, except the final tone line (up to three words from the brief), which is the one place a mood is allowed.
- Keep it under about 90 words. Detail that changes per shot belongs in the shots, not the DNA.
- Persistent weather or atmosphere (continuous rain, mist, water on the lens) goes in the DNA. Momentary events go in shots.
- Whatever the Style DNA says applies to every shot, so don't put a single-shot instruction in it.

```text
WEAK    Style DNA: dark, moody, cinematic, high quality, realistic.
STRONG  Style DNA: Shot on ARRI Alexa 35 with spherical primes. Locked-off. Single tungsten practical key, deep shadow…
WHY     Every slot is a mechanism the model can reproduce identically in every block.
```

## How to choose and adapt

1. Pick the preset closest to the brief's tone and the playbook.
2. Swap slots to fit the project (body, movement, key light, palette, atmosphere, tone words). Don't stack two presets.
3. Write it into the Bible under `STYLE DNA (LOCKED)`, then re-print the Bible.
4. Tell the user whether the preset is [Tested] or [General best practice].

---

## Tested presets (from the source workflow)

### 1. Bleak exterior — cinematic [Tested]
For survival, horror and dread exteriors, and rain or forest.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on ARRI Alexa 35 with anamorphic prime lenses. Handheld with subtle micro-shake. Photoreal live-action cinematography, no stylisation. Flat overcast key light, cold blue-grey ambience, deep crushed blacks, desaturated teal-green palette. Heavy continuous rain, volumetric mist between trunks, water beading on the lens. 24fps, 180-degree shutter, fine 35mm grain, shallow depth of field. Bleak, hopeless, oppressive.
```

### 2. Polished creator — persona [Tested]
For aspirational lifestyle and influencer content that's still handheld and human.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on Sony A7S III with a 35mm prime lens. Genuine handheld feel throughout — natural human hand tremor, small organic drifts and micro-adjustments in framing, not a locked tripod shot. Photoreal, not a digital render, not a 3D visualization. Warm amber shadows, cool blue-grey midtones, controlled highlights that never blow out, Kodak Vision3 250D character, subtle 35mm grain, soft halation around the practical light source. 30fps, real skin texture throughout, no beauty filter.
```

### 3. Raw phone UGC [Tested]
For reviews, testimonials and UGC ads, or anything that must look self-filmed.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on a recent smartphone. HDR, mild digital over-sharpening on edges, visible luminance noise in dim areas, slight rolling shutter on pans, clipped highlights near windows. Flat and ungraded. Genuine handheld feel throughout — natural human hand tremor, small organic drifts and micro-adjustments, slightly crooked horizons. Never a tripod, never a gimbal, never slow motion. Real room tone. No music. No film grain, no halation, no cinematic grade.
```
Adapting it: if the project mixes handheld and propped-phone shots, change "Genuine handheld feel throughout" to "Handheld or propped on a surface — real hand tremor when held, static but slightly crooked when propped", then lock it.

### 4. Clean industrial — car / product [Tested]
For cars, tech, metal and controlled premium spots.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on ARRI Alexa 35 with spherical prime lenses. Smooth controlled dolly movement. Photoreal live-action cinematography, no stylisation. Hard directional key light from camera-right, cool blue-grey fill, deep blacks, desaturated steel and graphite palette. 24fps, 180-degree shutter, fine 35mm grain, shallow depth of field on inserts, deep focus on wides. Cold, precise, controlled.
```

---

## General best-practice presets (not tested in this workflow)

### 5. Neo-noir night city [General best practice]
For thrillers, music videos and night chases.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on ARRI Alexa 35 with anamorphic prime lenses. Slow tracking moves and locked-off frames. Photoreal live-action cinematography, no stylisation. Practical neon signs and sodium-vapour streetlights as the only sources, magenta and cyan pools on wet asphalt, deep blacks, orange highlights against cyan shadows. Light rain, reflections in every surface, soft horizontal lens flares. 24fps, 180-degree shutter, fine 35mm grain, shallow depth of field. Lonely, electric, tense.
```

### 6. Warm 16mm nostalgia [General best practice]
For memories, coming-of-age stories, family stories and summer.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on 16mm film with vintage spherical primes. Handheld, gentle drifting movement. Photoreal live-action footage, no stylisation. Low golden-hour sun from behind the subject as the key, warm bounce fill. Lifted milky blacks, golden midtones, soft halation on highlights, slightly faded greens. Dust in the light, occasional soft lens flare. 24fps, 180-degree shutter, visible 16mm grain and gentle gate weave, shallow depth of field. Tender, sunlit, fleeting.
```

### 7. Single-source horror [General best practice]
For horror teasers, suspense and found-footage-adjacent work.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on ARRI Alexa 35 with spherical prime lenses. Slow, locked-off frames and creeping push-ins. Photoreal live-action cinematography, no stylisation. One small practical source per shot — a phone screen, torch or bare bulb — everything else falling to near-black, faint cold moonlight through windows. Desaturated cold palette, crushed blacks, skin slightly sallow. Still air, faint dust in the beam. 24fps, 180-degree shutter, fine 35mm grain, shallow depth of field. Quiet, wrong, dreadful.
```

### 8. Luxury product macro [General best practice]
For beauty, jewellery, fragrance and watches.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on ARRI Alexa 35 with a 100mm macro and spherical primes. Slow slider and motion-control moves. Photoreal live-action product cinematography, no stylisation, NOT a 3D render. Large soft top light with black flags for contrast, thin edge lights tracing contours, small controlled specular highlights. Neutral whites, rich deep blacks, true-to-life product colour. Fine mist or droplets on surfaces where specified. 24fps, 180-degree shutter, very fine grain, extremely shallow depth of field on details. Precise, sensual, quiet.
```

### 9. Sunlit lifestyle — food and drink [General best practice]
For cafés, kitchens, drinks and summer brands.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on ARRI Alexa 35 with spherical prime lenses. Handheld, light and steady. Photoreal live-action cinematography, no stylisation. Natural window daylight from camera-left as the key, warm bounce from a wooden table, backlight catching steam and condensation. Fresh natural colour, warm highlights, clean whites, soft contrast. 24fps, 180-degree shutter, fine grain, shallow depth of field. Fresh, warm, easy.
```

### 10. Documentary naturalism [General best practice]
For brand documentaries, behind-the-scenes, social realism and explainers with people.
```
Style DNA:
Shot on Sony FX6 with a 24–70mm zoom. Handheld observational camera, small reframes and focus pulls as if following real events. Photoreal, NOT a digital render. Available light only — windows, overheads, practicals — slightly uneven exposure. Natural colour with neutral white balance, gentle contrast, highlights allowed to clip a little. 25fps, 180-degree shutter, light digital noise, mixed depth of field. Honest, close, unpolished.
```

## Style DNA checks

- [ ] One preset adapted, not two stacked.
- [ ] Every slot is a mechanism; only the final tone line holds moods.
- [ ] Persistent atmosphere is in the DNA; momentary events are in the shots.
- [ ] It's locked in the Bible and pasted byte-identical into every block.
- [ ] Its label ([Tested] or [General best practice]) was told to the user.

<!-- Source: references/troubleshooting.md -->
**Source: references/troubleshooting.md**

# Troubleshooting

Diagnose before you rewrite. Most failures come from a reference problem, a vague mechanism, or a timing violation. **[Tested]** fixes are proven in this workflow; **[General best practice]** fixes are sound craft but untested here. Tell the user which is which.

## Diagnostic order

1. **References.** Is the upload order exactly the same as the Bible's @Image map? Is the right image in each slot? From block 2 on, is the previous block's last frame attached? [Tested]
2. **Locate the failure.** Find the exact block and timestamp. Fix that shot, not the whole prompt.
3. **Mechanism.** Is the failing moment described as visible mechanics, or as a mood or outcome? Make it a mechanism. [Tested]
4. **Wrong version.** Name the likely mistake inline ("does not throw it"). [Tested]
5. **Timing.** No shot under 2 s, no block over 30 s, and the durations total the block. [Tested]
6. **Style DNA.** Is it byte-identical to the other blocks? [Tested]
7. **Regenerate the failing block only**, keeping everything else fixed, so you learn what changed.

## Identity and faces

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Face changes between blocks | Upload order changed, or no last-frame reference | Restore the exact order; attach the previous block's final frame [Tested] |
| Blurry, averaged, "generic" face | Two full faces on the sheet, or several face references competing | Use a sheet with one full face (headless centre panel) [Tested]; add "One specific real person, not a composite. Do not beautify, smooth, or drift toward a generic face." [Tested] |
| Character renders headless or cropped in video | The headless centre panel is being copied | Add the face-source line: "take the face from the LEFT chest-up portrait panel. The centre panel omits the head deliberately. [Name] has a head and face in every shot." [Tested] |
| Plastic, waxy, airbrushed skin | Sheet too smooth, or a beauty bias | Run the skin realism pass on the sheet before video [Tested]; NEGATIVE: "no beauty filter, no CGI-smooth, waxy or airbrushed skin" [Tested] |
| Scar, tattoo or wound on the wrong side | The model mirrored the reference | State the side in capitals in every block: "the scar is on her LEFT cheek" [Tested] |

## Motion and morphing

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Character does two things at once | Two actions in one shot | Split into separate shots; sequence with "then" and a beat [Tested] |
| "Drops it" becomes a throw | Outcome verb, no mechanism | "hand goes limp, fingers uncurl, it slips from a slack grip — does not open the hand, does not throw it" [Tested] |
| Pose collapses early | Hold has no duration | "holds … for the full three seconds and does not lower the arm" [Tested] |
| Bodies, hands or objects morph mid-shot | Too much motion or too many changes in one shot; a shot too long for its action | One action per shot; shorten the shot or simplify the move; keep hands in simple, readable poses; avoid object-to-object contact in close-up [General best practice] |
| Glitchy flash shot | Shot under 2 s | Merge with the neighbour or extend to 3 s [Tested]; or group into a labelled montage segment [Tested] |
| Unwanted slow motion | The model's default for "cinematic" | "Never slow motion", in the CAMERA line and the NEGATIVE [Tested] |
| Gimbal-smooth UGC | No capture instructions | "filmed on a phone… real hand tremor… never a tripod, never a gimbal" [Tested] |
| Artifacts at block start or end | Normal edge artifacts | Keep key action away from the first and last ~0.5 s; trim 10–15 frames in the edit [Tested] |

## Products and text

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Product shape or colour changes | No product reference, or not declared | Give the product its own @Image slot; "Match exactly: [shape, colour, label]" in every block [Tested] |
| Label text warps or misspells | Fast motion, extreme angles, hands over the label, long text | Short label on the reference; label facing camera and steady, or slightly soft in the background; no fast rotation of the product; legible text added in the edit [General best practice]. Placing the wordmark toward camera but slightly out of focus kept it stable in production [Tested pattern] |
| Random captions, watermarks, logos appear | Default social-video bias | NEGATIVE: "No on-screen text, captions or graphics. No real-world brand logos. No watermark." [Tested] |

## Lip-sync, voice and audio

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Mouth moves badly while the character walks | Dialogue overlaps action | Speaker stops, then speaks; or convert to "Voiceover, no lip sync" over the action [Tested] |
| Lips move during a voiceover shot | Voiceover not labelled, or the face is in close shot | Label "Voiceover, no lip sync"; use hands-only or back-of-head framing for voiceover shots [Tested pattern] |
| Line out of sync or rushed | Line too long for the shot | Speaking segments under 8 s [Tested]; give each line its own shot with breathing room [General best practice] |
| Robotic, synthetic voice | No voice spec | "a natural, warm, human [female/male] voice, casual conversational cadence, real pitch variation, small natural imperfections. Must sound like an actual person, NOT synthetic or robotic." [Tested] |
| Unwanted music | Model adds a score | "No music." in AUDIO and NEGATIVE [Tested] |
| Silence gets filled | Silence not specified | "No dialogue from 3 to 6 s — only [sounds]. That silence is deliberate; do not fill it." [Tested pattern] |

## Look and continuity

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Looks like a 3D render or a video game | No realism clause; stylised words | "This must read as actual footage shot on a real camera, NOT a digital render, NOT a 3D visualization, NOT a video game environment." [Tested] |
| Look shifts between blocks | Style DNA reworded | Re-paste it byte-identical [Tested]; one grade adjustment layer in the edit [Tested] |
| Location changes between blocks | No plate, or not referenced | Same plate in every block: "match @ImageN's [light], palette and contrast exactly" [Tested] |
| Wardrobe reappears or changes | State not restated | CONTINUITY line: current state, plus what must not appear; add it to NEGATIVE [Tested pattern] |
| Prop changes hands | Hand not stated | "the cup is in her RIGHT hand", every block [Tested principle] |
| Extra people appear | Not excluded | "No other people." in NEGATIVE [Tested] |
| Film grain on a phone look | Default film-texture bias | "No film grain, no halation, no cinematic grade" [Tested] |
| Lighting doesn't match the plate | Video re-invents the light | Repeat the plate's named source in the block's location line [Tested pattern] |

## When nothing works

- Simplify the shot: fewer moving parts, a static camera, one action.
- Split the block into two shorter blocks at a beat.
- Re-check the reference images themselves, since a weak sheet causes every downstream failure. Regenerate it before regenerating video.
- Tell the user honestly when something is beyond what this workflow has tested, and suggest a small test generation.
